This is a working operating guide for Nightlife Culture. It helps people and AI-assisted production systems make consistent decisions without flattening the intelligence, culture or complexity of the work.

00How to use this guide

This guide has three layers. Use the first to understand what Nightlife Culture stands for, the second to express it consistently, and the third to produce accessible, evidence-led outputs.

LayerPurposeHow stable is it?
Brand foundationDefines our territory, beliefs, offer, audiences and method.Relatively stable. Review when the business proposition changes.
Expression systemDefines voice, tone, language, visual identity and imagery.Evolves through use, feedback and commissions.
Production systemDefines accessibility, evidence, documents, decks, spreadsheets, charts and AI controls.Operational and testable. Update when standards or tools change.

Decision hierarchy

When instructions compete, use this order:

  1. Legal and ethical requirements
  2. Accessibility and user need
  3. Factual and methodological integrity
  4. Clarity and usability
  5. Format conventions
  6. Brand consistency
  7. Stylistic preference

Accessibility does not dilute the brand. It decides where the brand should live.

Voice is not stylistic preference. The argument, the reasoning and culturally significant language sit with factual and methodological integrity, not at the bottom of this list. What comes last is decoration: a word choice that changes nothing.

Original thinking is not raw material to be sanitised

When you work from Carly's notes, recordings, transcripts or writing, preserve the argument before you touch the expression. Work from the originals, not from someone's summary of them.

  • Don't swap a distinctive explanation for conventional sector terminology.
  • Don't shrink an extended argument into a generic statement because the statement is shorter.
  • Don't trade a challenging position for a diplomatic one unless the context genuinely calls for it.
  • Keep the distinctions, qualifications, humour, analogies and examples.
  • Say which words are Carly's exact words, which are edited quotations and which are newly drafted.
  • Learn how she argues, then write new work that sounds like her. Lifting her lines is not the same thing.

The aim isn't to make Carly sound like a professional policy advisor. She already is one. It's to get her thinking across with the clarity, authority and personality she brings to a room.

Where the values live

This guide is the statement of the system. The values themselves — colours, the type voices, sizes and styles, the line weights, the slide patterns and the rules with their tiers — live once, in the design-system repository (foundations/tokens.json, foundations/rules.json, foundations/patterns.json), and everything else, this page included, is built from them. Where this guide and the repository disagree, the repository is current and this guide is behind.

01Brand foundation

What Nightlife Culture is

Nightlife Culture is a creative policy, research and design studio working across nightlife, music, culture, place and the systems that shape them.

We combine cultural literacy, lived experience, policy knowledge, evidence and human-centred design to help places and cultural ecosystems understand value, align people, make stronger decisions and build practical routes forward.

Short proposition

A creative policy studio for nightlife, music, culture and cities.

Long proposition

We help places and cultural ecosystems understand what creates value, what conventional systems miss, and what conditions people need to thrive. We turn lived experience, sector knowledge, data and creative practice into evidence, shared asks, practical frameworks and delivery routes.

The core belief

Nightlife is culture. It is made by artists, promoters, DJs, producers, crews, venue and festival teams, bar and door teams, technicians, audiences, organisers, freelancers, communities and informal networks.

Nightlife spaces are not passive backdrops. They are talent incubators, knowledge banks, gathering places, workplaces, testing grounds, civic assets and cultural value generators.

What we are building

Nightlife Culture is not defined by a conventional category alone. It can perform functions associated with consultancy, research, advocacy, convening, service design and policy development. The distinctive proposition is the combination: a studio practice that gathers people, builds evidence, makes value visible and designs practical routes forward.

What we're here to change

The systems that decide about nightlife mostly count what's easy to count: buildings, capacity, licences, turnover. So that's what they see. We challenge the measures, the assumptions and the processes that keep the rest out of view, and we design better ones with the people they're meant to serve.

Not to win the argument about what's broken. To change what happens next.

Our territory

We work where these areas meetTypical questions
Nightlife, music and cultureWhat creates value, identity, belonging, opportunity and collective joy?
Economic development and placeHow do culture and the night contribute to local growth, high streets, employment and investment?
Policy, planning and governanceWhere are rules, institutions, incentives and responsibilities misaligned with lived reality?
Public health, safety and accessWhat conditions help people participate, work and travel safely and with dignity?
Evidence, evaluation and dataWhat is counted, what is missing, and what can be known responsibly?
Human-centred and systems designHow can people shape decisions, tools and infrastructure that affect them?

What good work leaves behind

  • clearer evidence
  • stronger shared language
  • better decisions
  • usable tools and frameworks
  • more capable relationships and networks
  • transparent assumptions and methods
  • a practical route to implementation

02The Nightlife Culture method

The method is flexible enough for research, strategy, policy, feasibility, economic development, service design and sector-building work. Not every commission uses every stage, but the logic should remain visible.

My practice brings together human-centred design thinking, restorative economics and participatory creative production.

StepWhat it means
Listen — gather the peopleHear lived experience, establish trust and agree what matters.
Map — see the systemConnect cultural activity, relationships, resources and power.
Ideate — shape possible answersDevelop shared priorities and responses to the needs people identify.
Prototype — make it tangibleBuild an early resource or intervention people can use and challenge.
Test — learn in the openExamine recognition, usefulness and action with the people involved.
Refine — improve the methodUse feedback and evidence to change the account and the approach.
Expand — let the idea travelAdapt what works with another place while preserving local identity.

A repeatable creative production practice, developed through decades of sector-led delivery.

Method principles

  • Do not treat participation as decoration.
  • Do not confuse data volume with evidence quality.
  • Do not claim neutrality where choices and values are involved.
  • Do not reduce cultural value to economic value, but do not ignore economic reality.
  • Make limitations, assumptions and disagreements visible.
  • Design recommendations around who can act, with what authority, resource and timeframe.

Think in systems. Speak in stories.

We move between the specific and the systemic, then come back to the specific to check the argument holds. A resident DJ playing twenty little gigs across a city. What happens when their regular venue closes? What do their line-ups tell us about the relationships holding a scene together? And why can't the way government measures cultural infrastructure see any of it? One familiar night out, turned into a serious question about networks. It's an editorial principle, not a slogan to repeat.

How we build an argument

We don't open with abstract declarations about the importance of culture. We begin with something real. A room full of people. A promoter making something happen. A venue that doesn't fit the accepted definition. A statistic that tells half the story. A policy process that's somehow become more complicated than the problem it was meant to solve.

Then we dig into the assumptions underneath it. We connect cultural knowledge with economics, policy, design, research and lived experience, and we look for the contradictions. Who's been left out? What does the evidence actually say? Are we even asking the right question? Sometimes the most useful thing we can do is challenge the brief itself.

And then we explore what becomes possible when we look at it differently. The point isn't to explain the world as it is. It's to help people imagine and build something better.

Observation → Assumption → Contradiction → Connection → Possibility → Action.

A diagnostic, not a formula. Start with the contradiction, or the possibility, or a story that only shows its hand at the end. What matters is that the reasoning survives the edit.

03Voice and tone

Nightlife Culture comes from inside the culture we're working to support. We've made the parties, stood on the dancefloors, built the communities, worked with the institutions and navigated the policies that shape what happens after dark.

Here's the thing. Nobody ever changed a funding decision with a paragraph that sounded like a planning consultation. So don't write one.

When you write for Nightlife Culture, you're writing for nightlife, to the people who decide about it. That's two jobs at once. Speak the system's language well enough that the spreadsheet can't ignore you. Never let it speak for you. The intelligence of nightlife doesn't need translating into institutional language to become legitimate. Our cultural knowledge is expertise, and we use evidence to strengthen it, not replace it.

Who's reading? A licensing officer who's been fighting our corner for ten years with no ammo. A funder who's never been out on a Thursday in their life. A promoter who'll clock in one sentence whether we actually get it. Write so all three keep reading.

  • Write from the floor, not the balcony. You're not the tour guide or the anthropologist. Nobody needs the dancefloor explained to them.
  • Lead with what's working. The story of the night is joy, and the evidence backs it up.
  • Say the big thing plainly, then prove it. If you've got a number, make it massive. If you've got a hunch, call it a hunch and go and test it.
  • Be generous. Arenas, trade bodies, councils: they're bringing people together too. We're not here to slag anyone off. We're here to show what everyone's missing.
  • Ask the question nobody else is asking. Then ask the next one. Question the assumptions, expose the contradictions, and connect things that don't usually get considered together.
  • Have a laugh. We take complex problems seriously without taking ourselves too seriously. Joy doesn't turn up in a lanyard.
  • Swear if it's appropriate. Not because you think it makes you look edgy.

We're here to change the conversation about nightlife, and help the people who make it happen shape what happens next. If what you've written could have been written about any sector, by anyone, bin it and start again.

Nightlife Culture should sound able to move between the dancefloor, the committee room, the funder meeting and the evidence base without losing the truth of the culture.

The emotional arc

Joy → value → evidence → action.

This is the direction of travel, not a compulsory running order. Start wherever the argument is strongest: a story, a contradiction, a number. Just make sure the reader comes away knowing what people and places create, what the system is missing, what the evidence says and what can happen next.

Rigour is not respectability

Intellectual rigour is not the same thing as institutional respectability. You don't need to write like an institution to show you understand how one works, and questioning the assumptions behind institutions is one of our strongest assets. Good writing still knows who's reading, gives enough context, owns its uncertainty and uses real examples. What it doesn't do is fake it: no borrowed slang, no chatty filler, no pretend intimacy.

Voice characteristics

CharacteristicWhat it meansAvoid
Culturally rootedWe understand nightlife from participation, not observation. We know the people, practices and relationships behind the statistics.Explaining the culture to itself, or performing authenticity.
Intellectually curiousWe follow unexpected connections, question assumptions and investigate what conventional analysis overlooks.Answering the brief without asking whether it's the right brief.
Plainspoken and preciseWe explain complex policy, economics and cultural theory without stripping out their meaning, and name evidence, uncertainty and structural problems accurately.Consultancy sludge, unsupported certainty or softened truth.
Provocative with purposeWe challenge conventional thinking and name structural problems, and we can defend the argument.Criticism for its own sake, or a challenge watered down into a diplomatic shrug.
Playful and irreverentWe have humour, character and a healthy disregard for unnecessary institutional pomposity. Humour exposes contradictions.Jokes that belittle communities or people with less power.
Generous and collaborativeWe recognise other people's knowledge, bring different perspectives together and create opportunities for collective action.Defining people or places only through failure or need.
Joyful and ambitiousWe see extraordinary possibilities in nightlife and believe they deserve serious consideration and investment.Empty optimism, or abundance framing that hides structural problems.
Restlessly practicalIdeas are there to be tested. We prototype, learn, adapt and build. We want things to happen.Ending on vague support or further engagement.

Three voice modes

Three registers of the same intellectual position, not three personalities.

ModeWhen to use itCharacter
Carly, the founderThought leadership, talks, opinion pieces, personal reflections, project introductionsFirst person, distinctive, curious, funny, opinionated and grounded in lived experience.
Nightlife Culture, the studioWebsite, proposals, collaborative projects, general communicationsCollective, confident, culturally rooted and evidence-led. Still has personality.
Nightlife Culture, the evidence and policy authorityResearch, technical documents, policy recommendations, investment cases and formal submissionsMethodologically rigorous, precise and transparent. The argument stays clear and culturally informed.

Professional never automatically means removing personality. And keep it honest: don't imply a large permanent team, or that a whole sector has agreed a position, when neither is true.

Voice stays; tone moves

The voice should remain recognisably Nightlife Culture. Tone changes according to audience, purpose, risk and format.

ContextToneWhat to emphasise
Public and sector communicationsDirect, warm, culturally literatePeople, place, lived reality, concrete meaning and action.
Policy and technical reportsPrecise, structured, evidence-ledDefinitions, methods, assumptions, classifications and feasibility.
Decision briefingsConcise, calm, decision-readyThe question, evidence, options, risks, recommendation and owner.
Funding and investmentAmbitious but groundedNeed, value, method, outcomes, governance and delivery confidence.
Research and academic workTransparent, rigorous, appropriately technicalSources, methods, limitations, reproducibility and interpretation.
Workshops and learningInvitational, clear, pacedPurpose, steps, examples, participation and usable takeaways.

04Language and editorial rules

Core language

Use these ideas where they are accurate, not as automatic slogans: collective joy; scenes; gathering places; cultural infrastructure; informal knowledge; trust, care and graft; conditions to thrive; people who make the night happen; shared asks; practical frameworks; sector knowledge; talent incubation; cultural value; evidence with soul.

These are ideas, not a phrasebook. The same goes for Carly's own images, like the spreadsheet guardians or the elephant burgers: they work because they come out of the argument. Sprinkle them in as decoration and the voice turns into a parody of itself.

Technical and policy language

Nightlife Culture does not avoid specialist, academic or policy language where it is the most accurate language for the job.

Terms such as regeneration, placemaking, resilience, creative industries, meanwhile use, stakeholder and ecosystem may have specific meanings within economic development, planning, research, funding and public policy. Use them where that meaning is relevant, particularly in technical reports, policy recommendations, planning documents, funding cases and work written for professional audiences.

The aim is not to simplify complex ideas until they lose their meaning. We can write with intellectual and methodological rigour while remaining clear, human and rooted in the people and places that make nightlife happen.

Plain English is not anti-intellectual. It makes meaning available without removing complexity.

Context-dependent language

Context testRule
Technical and professional documentsUse the recognised term when precision, comparability or alignment with policy requires it.
Public communicationsTranslate specialist language into clear, concrete language without losing the meaning.
Vague or contested termsSpecify who or what the term refers to, what action is proposed and who benefits.
Precision versus informalityDo not replace a precise term simply to sound informal. Do not use a technical term to sound authoritative.

Contested terms

TermUse it whenCheck for
VibrancyIt is defined through specific activity, time, place or indicator.Whether it is vague, exclusionary or visually coded.
ResilienceIt describes a system capacity, tested condition or defined risk.Whether responsibility is being shifted onto under-resourced people.
InnovationSomething is genuinely new or newly applied.Whether practical improvement would be more accurate.
InclusionThe group, barrier, mechanism and outcome are named.Whether the term hides unequal power or access.
RegenerationIt has a planning, funding or policy meaning relevant to the work.Who benefits, what may be displaced and whose place is being remade.
ActivationIt describes a specific intervention, use or programme.Whether it implies a place was empty before institutional action.
StakeholderIt is useful in technical governance or project documentation.Whether people, partners, residents, workers or sector voices would be more accurate.
CommunityA defined group, place or relationship is meant.Whether differences in interest and power are being hidden.
PlacemakingIt is a recognised planning or practice term needed for the audience.Whether it erases people already making and caring for the place.
EcosystemRelationships and interdependencies are genuinely being analysed.Whether it is replacing a more precise description.
World-classThere is a stated comparison and credible evidence.Unsupported boosterism.
Meanwhile useIt describes a specific temporary planning or property arrangement.Whether cultural users are expected to absorb insecurity for others' benefit.
Creative industriesThe official sector definition or policy category is relevant.Which subsectors and classifications are included or excluded.

Editorial standard

  • Establish the argument early, but leave room for a story, a discovery or a reveal.
  • Mix sentence lengths: long when you're exploring a relationship, short when you land the point.
  • Break long sentences where ideas compete.
  • Prefer concrete verbs to abstract nouns.
  • Use headings and short sections to guide the reader.
  • Use examples that are real and relevant.
  • Cut filler, accidental repetition and AI-style platitudes. Keep deliberate repetition: it's rhythm and conviction.
  • Do not invent specificity, statistics or quotes.
  • Keep nuance where it changes meaning.

Rhythm, emphasis and rhetoric

Nightlife Culture writing should have the energy and movement of a good conversation.

  • Questions are welcome when they expose an assumption, introduce real uncertainty or bring the reader into the reasoning. Often they're the most important part of the argument, so don't cut them just to sound more declarative. Questions used as empty hooks go.
  • Repetition can build emphasis and conviction. Remove the accidental kind, not the deliberate rhythm.
  • Humour, understatement and irreverence are part of the voice. Use them naturally, not as decoration.
  • Metaphors are there to clarify relationships and complex ideas, not to make ordinary writing sound creative.
  • Bring a big argument back to a simple, familiar image when you can.

House spellings

  • Night time is two words, never hyphenated: night time economy, Night Time Advisor. (Decided 4 October 2026; the design system's checks refuse the hyphen.)
  • Cultural value and cultural contribution are not interchangeable. Cultural value is what something is worth to people and places; cultural contribution is what a particular person, venue or scene adds. Use the one you mean.
  • British English throughout.

Avoid AI voice

Avoid formulaic phrases such as “this matters”, “here is the bit everyone misses”, “in today’s rapidly changing landscape”, “unlock the potential”, “at the heart of” and “more important than ever”, unless the wording is genuinely earned by the content. Avoid the patterns too: every argument turned into three short sentences, three abstract nouns or a predictable inspirational conclusion. That's the machine's rhythm, not ours.

What flattening looks like

What flattening looks like. The stronger versions aren't more aggressive. They're more specific, they have a point of view, and they're much harder to mistake for generic consultancy writing.

Cultural value

Flattened: Small venues make an important contribution to local cultural ecosystems.

Stronger: We tend to measure the importance of a venue by how many people it can fit through the door. But what if the most culturally significant room in a city only holds 75 people?

What if that's where the next musical movement is being made?

Perhaps the problem isn't the size of the venue. Perhaps we're measuring the wrong thing.

Evidence

Flattened: Nightlife Culture brings together existing datasets to strengthen evidence-led advocacy.

Stronger: We've got government datasets telling us one thing about a place and ticketing data telling us something completely different.

One tells us how many businesses and licensed premises exist. The other starts showing us what people are actually programming.

What happens when we put those two pictures together? And what might we find out about the people and places we've been overlooking?

Collaboration

Flattened: We take a collaborative, human-centred approach to policy development.

Stronger: I don't want to spend another three years consulting people about something they already know needs to change.

I want to get the right people in a room, work out what's stopping us, agree what we're going to test and get on with it.

And when we bring people back together, they should be able to see what changed because they were there.

06Evidence standard

Nightlife Culture’s credibility depends on how evidence is gathered, classified, interpreted and communicated. Strong design must never make weak evidence look stronger than it is.

  • Distinguish fact, estimate, interpretation, assumption and recommendation.
  • Cite the original source wherever possible.
  • State publication date, data period, geography and population.
  • Explain sector definitions and classifications, including SIC codes where relevant.
  • Identify proprietary, commercial and restricted data.
  • Describe primary research methods, recruitment, sample size and limitations.
  • Do not imply causation from correlation.
  • Avoid unsupported economic-impact multipliers and false precision.
  • Separate commissioned evidence from independent evidence.
  • Record uncertainty, missing data, disagreement and methodological judgement.
  • Link recommendations to evidence and identify who can act.

Accurate evidence, strong argument

Two different jobs. Accuracy is about the evidence: what it is, where it came from, what it can and can't carry. Strength is about the argument we make with it. A sharp argument can stand on modest evidence, as long as we're straight about which is which. What we never do is let a confident argument make the evidence look stronger than it is, or let cautious evidence talk us out of making the argument at all.

Source line

Every data visual, table or significant factual claim should enable the reader to trace the evidence. Link to the specific dataset, publication or page rather than an organisation homepage where possible.

Recommendation test

QuestionRequired answer
What is being recommended?A specific action, choice or principle.
Why?The evidence and reasoning.
Who can act?Named institution, role, partnership or sector.
What is required?Authority, funding, capacity, data, policy change or collaboration.
When?Timeframe or decision point.
How will we know?Outcome, indicator, review or learning mechanism.
What could go wrong?Risk, trade-off, unintended effect or dependency.

Relationship to the research methodology

This section is the communications-facing summary. The full standard — provenance codes, minimum source metadata, the indicator comparability gate, classification versioning, ethics and the recommendation strength scale — lives in Comparative Place-Based Research Methodology v1.0. Where the two documents touch, the methodology governs. Section 12 of this guide translates its requirements into chart and layout components.

The colour rule

Every accent takes ink text. Every ground takes the text colour its own token declares — white on blue and ink, ink on chalk and white. There is no single sentence covering all four grounds: white on chalk is 1.11:1 and white on white is 1.00:1, so read the pairing off the token, never from memory. The other failures stand as before — white on pink is 2.62:1, white on violet is 2.54:1, black on blue is 2.44:1.

v1.4.1 · The previous one-line law — “every ground is a white-text surface” — was false for chalk and white and is retired (register contradiction X-02).

Accent adjacency

Because the five accents share a lightness register, every pair sits between 1.01 and 1.98:1. They are distinguished by hue alone. In greyscale, on a projector, or for a reader with a colour vision deficiency they collapse into one another.

This is a deliberate trade — it is what makes the palette harmonious. It means:

  • The accents are a surface palette, not a data palette. Charts use the ramp in section 12, never these.
  • Roles, not adjacency, keep them apart. Pink is the small hot mark, teal the cool highlight, violet the calm surface, butter the warm one, coral the urgent one. Give each a job and they never need to be told apart at a glance.
  • Two accents never sit edge to edge carrying different meanings without a separator or a label.

Colour rule

Colour is never the only carrier of meaning. Test every foreground and background combination. Use WCAG thresholds: at least 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text, and 3:1 for meaningful graphics and interface components.

  • Do not reduce opacity on essential text.
  • Do not place essential text directly over photography without a tested solid surface.
  • Make links identifiable by more than colour alone.
  • Pair status colours with words, symbols or patterns.
  • Use the chart ramp rather than assuming the brand accents can do every job.
  • Protect functional interface colours and visible focus states from decorative brand overrides.

Note on the 3:1 graphics threshold. It applies to graphics required to understand content and to interface components. A coloured panel that is simply a surface holding high-contrast text is neither — the text carries the contrast. Panel outlines are a style choice, not an accessibility requirement. The threshold does apply to chart series, meaningful icons and strokes, focus states, and any edge that itself carries meaning.

08Typography

Five voices, six sizes, twenty-six named styles. A component may place text, colour it and put a line beside it; it never sets a typeface, a size, a weight or capitals of its own.

One rule for all type

Every text style in the system is one voice at one size, and every one has a name that says what it is. The voices are the faces as the brand uses them; the sizes are six steps and no others; the styles are the pairings a document needs, each with the Word style it becomes. The web stylesheet, the component library and the Word styles are generated from the same table (foundations/tokens.json), so they cannot disagree, and the build refuses a component that sets its own type. Decided 5 October 2026.

The name is the class in HTML and the style in Word. A heading style sits only on its own element, h1 to h4. H4 is the floor: there is no H5 or H6. If content seems to need one, it needs a new section, a list or a table. Captions under charts and figures, source lines and notes under tables are the small style; a label is a phrase, never a sentence.

The caps rule

All-caps headings are core to how Nightlife Culture looks. They also carry a readability cost, which falls hardest on dyslexic and low-vision readers. The rule is caps with guardrails, not caps with an exception:

  • Always tracked. Every caps voice carries a letter-spacing value. That is the mitigation, not a styling preference — untracked caps are measurably harder to read.
  • Never below 16pt for a heading. Below that, caps lose the word-shape cues that make scanning possible. The only capitals under the floor are the fixed small styles in Table 8.2: titles in contents and tables at 14px (10.5pt), and the label voice and numbers at 12px (10pt).
  • Eight words maximum, two lines maximum. Caps are for statements, not sentences.
  • H3, H4 and everything in the text voice stay sentence case. In a long report, all-caps sub-headings are tiring and the brand gains least at that level.
  • Never caps in body copy, notes, source lines, alt text or table cells. A table's title and its header row are capitals.

Screen readers handle capitalised words correctly when the caps are applied as formatting. Caps are never typed: use text-transform: uppercase in HTML and the All Caps character format in Word and PowerPoint. Typed capitals destroy the underlying string for search, copy-paste, translation and some assistive-technology configurations — and the damage is invisible in the rendered result, so it survives every visual review. Tracked, short and above 16pt, caps are defensible. Untracked and long, they are not.

Typographic rules

  • Left-align body text. Do not justify.
  • Italic for a short run inside a paragraph: a quoted phrase, a title, a word. A true italic is embedded for it. Bold inside a paragraph is rare; bold is for the first column of a table. (A logged departure from the Decision Book's avoid-italics rule, DOC-14, decided 4 October 2026.)
  • Reserve underlining for links and the text action beside a button.
  • No monospace anywhere. Figures are Inter with tabular figures. A file name or literal string is the file-reference style: a white hairline chip in Inter.
  • Use 12pt body text in documents, with 1.5 to 1.6 line spacing in running prose. Other style classes set their own — see below.
  • Remove copy before reducing type.

Readable size rules

FormatMinimumPreferred
Slide titles32pt38–52pt
Slide body18pt20–26pt
Slide labels14pt16pt+
Document body12pt12pt
Footnotes and caveats10pt10.5–11pt. A caveat that matters belongs in the title, column heading or row label, not a footnote. A caveat that does not matter should be deleted.

Line height is scoped, not one number

WCAG SC 1.4.8 sets 1.5 as the floor for line spacing within paragraphs. It was never a rule about table cells, slide bullets, captions or headings. Applied as a blanket it produces two specific failures: display type at 1.5 reads limp, and a table at 1.5 stops scanning across, because rows are read horizontally and generous leading pulls them apart.

Style classDocumentHTMLSlideWhy
Display, H11.02–1.11.02–1.11.02–1.1Tight leading is what makes display type read as a unit.
H2, H31.15–1.251.2–1.31.15–1.25Short lines; leading is spacing, not readability.
Running prose1.5–1.61.5–1.61.25–1.4The only place SC 1.4.8 applies. Slides rarely carry paragraphs.
Slide body, bullets——1.2–1.35Few lines, short measure, read at distance.
Table cells1.25–1.351.25–1.351.2–1.3Not paragraphs. Tight is more readable — rows must stay scannable.
Captions, source lines1.3–1.41.3–1.41.25–1.35Short, secondary, one or two lines.
Statistic blocks1.0–1.11.0–1.11.0–1.1A number is not text.
Lists1.4–1.51.4–1.51.25–1.35Space between items does the work.

Only the running-prose row is Fixed. Everything else is Adaptable — the rule is that the value is scoped, not that these particular numbers are correct. The same scoping applies to measure, minimum size and alignment.

Font delivery

Archivo Black, Archivo and Inter are open-licence (SIL Open Font License). Embed them in every digital deliverable — never link them from a web font service. A linked font fails silently and falls back to a system sans, which is how a deck can look wrong on someone else's machine without anyone noticing. Where a font cannot be embedded, the approved fallback stack is Arial, then the system sans.

09Layout and containment

Contain with colour and space, not with outlines.

Panels are held by fill, rule or space. Hard black outlines are retired — they were doing the work that space should do, and they made every panel shout at the same volume.

No border

Fill. The colour field is the container. The default for accent panels. Needs space around it.

Top rule

Top rule. White panel, callout line. Dense pages, tables and long documents.

Left rule

Left rule. Reads as an aside rather than a box. Pull quotes and callouts.

Full-bleed band

Band. Runs edge to edge. Stops being a panel and becomes a change of ground.

Hairline

Hairline. 1px ink at 22%. White boxes on chalk, tables, dense reference layouts.

Table 9.1 · The containment treatments
TreatmentSpecUse
FillAccent background, no borderDefault for accent panels. Requires generous surrounding space.
Top ruleWhite panel, callout line (8px) on topDense pages, tables, long documents where five filled panels would be too much. The key statement a section turns on.
Left ruleWhite panel, callout line (8px) on the leftCallouts, asides, a recommendation and why, a working note.
Full-bleed bandAccent or ink, edge to edgeSlides and covers. How an accent leads without looking like a box.
Hairline1px ink at 22%White panels on a chalk ground, tables, forms. Never for anything carrying meaning.
Hard outline—Retired.

Four weights of line

A line is one of four weights and no others. A line that goes with text is a rule; a line on a filled box is a callout line, double the rule. Each weight is double the one before and all four are in Word's own border menu. Decided 5 October 2026, replacing eleven weights that had grown up by accident.

Table 9.2 · The four weights
WeightScreenPrintWhat it is for
Hairline1px0.75ptTable rows, contents rows, outlines, the foot of a page. Never carries meaning (NC-CON-02).
Table2px1.5ptUnder a table's header row. Half the rule, in proportion to the 12px headings it sits under.
Rule4px3ptA line that goes with text: section title, H4 bar, breaker, rail marker, quotation, comparability flag.
Callout8px6ptA line on a filled box, at the top or the left: key statement, callout, recommendation, Claude note, statistic, chart card, accent table.

Quotes, statements and notes

  • Takeaway — one or two sentences to remember, bold, in the running text with a pink rule. Quotation — the same frame at regular weight. Both at body size, with the attribution in the label voice beneath. Not necessarily boxed.
  • Key statement — the question or point a section turns on: bold, at body size, in a top-rule panel. It is never larger than the heading above it; the panel does the pulling out.
  • Subtitle — the line under a title, Inter Regular at 18px, so a subtitle is never mistaken for a sub-section.
  • Evidence mark — the label voice in square brackets inside a sentence: [Measured · internal analytics].
  • Recommendation — a left-rule panel in blue with a blue chip reading Recommendation, then the recommendation and why.
  • Working note — a left-rule panel in coral, labelled as not for publication. It never prints.

Status, controls and headings that open

Added from the first long interactive document built on the system (the dashboard-design reader, October 2026).

  • Status chips are the label voice on a fill, one accent per state: To do violet, In progress butter, Review pink, Blocked coral, Done teal, Parked white, Proposed butter. Agreed and Your answer are the inverse of the ground. Recommendation is blue, and ink on a blue ground. The word carries the meaning, never the colour alone. Public severity marks are not decided (section 15).
  • One button: blue, fully rounded, sentence case, the one thing to press; on a blue ground it is white with blue wording. A minor action beside it is the same voice, underlined. One search field: white with a hairline, a charcoal hint, a blue focus ring and an icon button.
  • Any heading may open and close. It keeps the style of its level and its content sits in line with it. A heading that holds the finding starts open. Everything prints open.
  • Contents: titles in capitals with a line of Inter beneath, the chapter number in the same ink box as a section title, the page number in the number style with a p. The rail is the same list with a rule-weight marker on the current chapter.
  • On ink and blue, every text style, label and link is white. The number box and the line under a section title stay teal, as the line above a slide title does.

Layout rules

  • One main idea per slide or section where possible.
  • Use space as part of the voice.
  • Use blue as a structural signal rather than scattered decoration.
  • Avoid dense boxes, tiny labels and decorative clutter.
  • Keep core information in a simple reading order.
  • Use single-column layouts for long-form accessible documents where practical.
  • Chalk ground, white panels. Or white ground, panels held by a rule.

10Slides

Slides are built from twelve patterns taken from real Nightlife Culture decks. Pick the pattern by what the slide has to do. Each one is shown here as the design system builds it.

If no pattern fits, build the slide from the same parts (titles, columns, rules, filled boxes, callouts, bands) and add it as a new pattern with the real slide it came from. Never invent sizes or colours.

Two kinds of slide

KindRule
Statement — cover, statementOne idea. Most of the slide stays empty.
Working — every other patternA title, a lead and up to eight short blocks. If it does not fit at the sizes below, it is two slides. Remove copy before reducing type.

Grounds

GroundTitles and headingsUse
BlueWhite titles, teal headingsCovers, statements, and slides that need to land.
ChalkBlue titles and headings, ink textWorking slides. White in reports and print.
InkWhite titles, teal headingsThe dark ground for presentations. Never charcoal, never grey.
AccentsInk textRules, filled boxes and side blocks. Never a whole slide.

Which ground, for which room. Light ground is the default whenever the venue is unconfirmed. Ambient light lifts a projector's blacks, so an ink deck greys out in a lit room; ink needs a darkened room, confirmed in advance.

Sizes

ElementSizeNote
Title43.3pt36pt for a long title. Caps, three lines maximum.
Statement and cover titles60pt · 70.7pt
Lead19.5ptLarger for a statement: 23, 27.4 or 36pt.
Column heading20.9ptBlue on light, teal on dark.
Body18ptThe floor for projected text.
Label18ptCaps, tracked.
Table12ptOnly in decks that are sent and read, not projected.

Side margins 5.25% of the slide width. The title sits 6.7% from the top. Content stops 8% above the foot, or above a closing band. Measured on a 13.33-inch slide.

Slide numbers

Two-digit, bottom-right, 16pt bold. Ink on light grounds, teal on dark grounds and on a closing band. Content slides only — not the cover, not the closing slide. Numbered by position in the deck, not by section. People cite slides in meetings, funders and officers reference them in writing, and decks get printed and reordered.

11Logo

The wordmark is an outlined asset. It is never re-set as live type.

That sentence is the whole rule. Everything below explains why, so nobody is tempted to fudge it.

The files

FileUse
nightlife-culture-wordmark.svgInline in HTML. Inherits currentColor — set color on the parent.
nightlife-culture-wordmark-white.svgOn blue, ink, or any dark ground. For <img>.
nightlife-culture-wordmark-blue.svgOn chalk or white. For <img>.
nightlife-culture-wordmark-ink.svgOn an accent ground. For <img>.

All four are outlined vector paths. They render identically whether or not Archivo Black is installed. currentColor does not work through <img> — use a coloured variant there.

Why it must not be re-set

The wordmark comes from the printed business card. Measured from that artwork:

MeasureValue
NIGHTLIFE32.09pt
CULTURE33.41pt
Rendered width, NIGHTLIFE171.92pt
Rendered width, CULTURE171.19pt
Baseline to baseline30.41pt
Effective line-height0.9476

The two lines are set at different sizes so they justify to the same width — 171.92 against 171.19, a difference of 0.4%. That is what makes the lockup read as a solid rectangle rather than a ragged stack.

Set both lines at one size and you lose it. Every regenerated version has made exactly that mistake, including the nightlife-culture-lockup.svg in the design-system development folder, which is live <text> at a single size with letter-spacing:-3 — a rendering of type, not the mark.

If a future version looks almost right, this is why.

Rules

  1. Never re-set as live type. Not in HTML, not in PowerPoint, not in Figma, not in a prompt. Place the SVG.
  2. Never restack, re-space or re-track it. The relationship between the two lines is the mark.
  3. Never stretch it. Scale proportionally. No preserveAspectRatio="none", no dragging a corner without a modifier key.
  4. One colour only. The defaults: white on blue and ink, blue on chalk and white, ink on an accent. The two-colour treatment (charcoal + one accent) is permitted on covers only.
  5. Any accent may carry the wordmark, on any ground. Logo colour is a brand choice, not text: a logotype is exempt from text-contrast rules (WCAG 1.4.3), so this is a deliberate, logged break (design system rule NC-BRK-03), not an oversight.
  6. Clear space: at least the cap height of NIGHTLIFE on all four sides. Nothing enters it.
  7. Minimum size: 90px wide on screen, 22mm in print. Below that, use the wordmark on one line or omit it.
  8. Never place it on photography without a tested solid surface behind it.
  9. Never add anything to it — no strapline locked up, no box, no rule, no shadow, no outline.
  10. Never two logos on one surface.

Ground and variant

Each swatch below is a ground, not a specimen. No wordmark is drawn on this page, because drawing one here would mean re-setting it as type — the exact thing rule 1 forbids. The slot shows where the placed SVG goes and which file to use.

wordmark-blue.svg

Chalk or white ground. Blue wordmark. The footer default.

wordmark-white.svg

Blue ground. White wordmark by default. Any accent is allowed.

wordmark-white.svg

Ink ground. White wordmark.

wordmark-ink.svg

Accent ground. Ink wordmark. Two-colour (charcoal + one accent) is permitted on covers only, never in a footer.

Placement

WhereRule
Slides — cover, dividers, closingFull lockup.
Slides — contentNo logo by default. The exception is any slide likely to travel alone — a headline finding, a data slide, a quote. If you would screenshot it, mark it.
Slide footer versionApproximately 1.5% of slide width. It should be the quietest thing there.
DocumentsCover and back page only. Never in a running header.
Everything elseOnce. Quietly.

If you need something this section does not cover: say so and stop. Do not improvise a variant. A logo that gets improvised is not a logo.

This document

The masthead and footer now carry the placed outlined wordmark, inline, inheriting currentColor. Earlier versions set them as live Archivo Black at a single size — the exact failure described above, in the guide's own furniture.

The four SVGs were regenerated from the measurements in this section and verified against them: NIGHTLIFE renders at 171.92pt, CULTURE at 171.19pt, the two lines justifying to within 0.42%. Tracking differs per line by design (−0.0872em and −0.0264em) — that is what makes two different sizes finish at the same width.

If a regenerated mark does not reproduce those two widths, it is not the mark. Do not ship it.

12Data and charts

The brand accents cannot carry data. This ramp can — the same hues, stepped in lightness so the series stay distinct in greyscale, on a projector and for a colourblind reader.

The chart ramp

#0000FF
#C7339A
#00C6C5
#FFDE6B

The grey strip is the same four series desaturated. Lightness climbs monotonically (0.45 → 0.58 → 0.75 → 0.91), so the order survives photocopying, greyscale printing, projection, deuteranopia and tritanopia. Under protanopia the order inverts: series 1 and 2 converge to 1.10:1, effectively one colour. Wherever both appear in the same chart, differentiate them by more than colour — a dashed stroke, a marker, or a direct label. The label-at-the-mark rule already covers most cases. The brand accents do not have this property and cannot, if they are to stay harmonious.

SeriesHexOKLCH LLabels
Series 1#0000FF0.45White
Series 2#C7339A0.58White
Series 3#00C6C50.75Ink
Series 4#FFDE6B0.91Ink

Chart rules

RuleWhy
Four series maximumBeyond four the ramp stops being distinguishable. Five categories means a bar chart with direct labels, not more colours.
One series = blueThe ramp is for genuinely different series. A single-series chart in four colours implies a distinction that is not there.
Label at the markValues on bars, series names at the end of lines, percentages in the key. Legends are a last resort.
Never brand accentsPink, teal, violet, butter and coral are surfaces. Only the ramp encodes data.
Show the gapsHatched fill for suppressed, dashed line for a break in collection. Never a silent omission — a gap in the data is a finding.
Show the rangeModelled or surveyed values get a visible interval. A bare point estimate reads as a count.
Provenance on every chartCode, reference period, geography and boundary vintage.
Flag illustrative figuresAny placeholder or worked example says so, in the chart, every time.
Gridlines at 10% inkPresent enough to read against, quiet enough to disappear. Never heavier than the data.
Alt text describes the findingNot “line chart of venue counts” but what the chart shows. Plus a data table alternative for anything load-bearing.
No non-uniform scalingAn SVG or image never gets stretched to fit. The container flexes; the coordinate space does not. Stretching destroys the type.
Separator on segmented formsDonuts and 100% stacked bars have segments that touch. Adjacent ramp contrast in greyscale is 1.79, 2.27 and 1.61 — all below the 3:1 threshold for meaningful graphics. A 1–2px white or ink hairline between adjacent segments closes it. The ramp is rated for separated, labelled marks; not for shared edges.

Chart types

TypeWhen
Ranked horizontal barThe workhorse. Categories with a magnitude. Ranked descending unless the categories have a natural order.
Dot plotComparing places. Bars imply a quantity from zero; dots imply a position on a scale, which is what an indicator is — and leave room for the plausible range.
100% stacked barComparing two or more wholes. Replaces most pies.
DonutOne whole, four segments maximum, percentages always in the key. The hole carries the total.
PiePermitted, with the caveat that angles are read less accurately than lengths. Justified when one dominant share needs to be instantly recognisable. Same four-segment limit.
LineChange over time. Series labelled at the line, never in a legend. Dashed segments for breaks in collection — never interpolate across one.
Range barAnywhere uncertainty is material.

Worked example — single series, blue, labelled at the mark

Venues82
Artists64
Promoters47
Crew & tech[c]

[c] suppressed for disclosure control. The row stays; the gap is visible. ADM-OPEN 2025 · LA boundary 2023 · illustrative figures.

Tables

Demonstration and reference tables are two different objects. This is a demonstration table — small, in the flow, supporting the sentence beside it. A reference table belongs in a spreadsheet. Editorial is the default: no fill, no vertical rules, no outer border.

Table 1 · Where value is held in the night time economy, by actor
ActorShare of valueIndexChange
VenuesPremises turnover, licensed trade82.4+4.1
ArtistsFees, recording, publishing64.0−2.3
PromotersTicketing margin, production47.2+1.8
Crew and techFreelance and agency labour[c]n/a

The title above is the table-title style; the header row is the label voice under the 2px table line; the first column is bold, because it names the row. Figures are Inter with tabular figures, right-aligned with their column headings, so digits line up by place value. Consistent precision within each column. Rows ordered by the data, largest first — not alphabetically. [c] suppressed for disclosure control; n/a not collected. Never a blank cell, because a gap in the data is a finding.

Presentations use the slide table instead: see the Table pattern in section 10.

Evidence furniture

These components come from Comparative Place-Based Research Methodology v1.0. They are not decorative.

Provenance chips

OFF-OPENADM-OPENADM-RESTRICTEDACADEMICPRI-OPEN
SECTORCOM-DOCUMENTEDPRI-DOCUMENTED
COM-PARTIALCOM-BLACKBOXPRI-OPAQUEANECDOTALUNTRACEABLE

Three tiers: ink for open and traceable, butter for documented-but-partial, coral for opaque or untraceable. The code text carries the meaning on its own, so the tier survives greyscale and screen readers. Coral does not mean “bad” — it means “handle with a stated caveat”.

Comparability flag

Any chart comparing two or more places states whether the indicator comparability gate has been cleared, and which of the eight criteria required harmonisation. A comparison without this note is not publishable.

Recommendation strength

The 1–5 scale shown as filled ordinal steps in ink, never as a colour scale — strength is ordinal, so it is shown by how much is filled. Readable in greyscale, and it cannot be mistaken for a red/amber/green judgement. The level is always written out alongside.

Statistic blocks

Every big number carries a source line by default: reference period, geography, boundary vintage and provenance code. A statistic without them is a claim, not a finding, and the evidence standard separates the two.

13Accessibility standard

Accessibility is a design standard, not finishing polish.

When brand and accessibility conflict, accessibility wins. Move the brand to layout, rhythm, typography, covers, pattern, photography or non-essential decoration rather than weakening the meaning layer.

Fixed, adaptable and decorative

ClassExamplesRule
FixedSemantic headings, readable size, contrast, links, reading order, focus states, alt textDo not override for brand preference.
AdaptableLogo scale, exact colour tint, spacing, page composition, chart stylingAdjust to user, format and accessibility needs.
DecorativePatterns, textures, overlays, flourishes, non-informational imageryMay be removed without losing meaning.

Minimum rules

  • Meet WCAG 2.2 AA as the minimum standard; aim higher where practical.
  • Choose the format from the user need, not production habit.
  • Publish HTML first for public information where practical.
  • Use real headings, lists and table structures.
  • Use descriptive links, never “click here”.
  • Add useful alt text to meaningful images and mark decorative images appropriately.
  • Do not use images of text when live text will work.
  • Provide text or data alternatives for charts and diagrams.
  • Check reading order before PDF publication.
  • Set document title and language metadata.
  • Test with automated checks and manual review.

Disclosure control

[c] already marks a suppressed value. This is the rule that decides when to use it.

  • No published figure rests on fewer than three contributing units.
  • Where a cell falls below the threshold, suppress it and apply secondary suppression, so the value cannot be recovered by subtraction from row or column totals.
  • Keep category structures fixed across editions. Two differently-cut tables of the same population can be differenced against each other to recover what neither shows.
  • If more than half a table is suppressed, change the geography or the categories rather than publishing holes.
  • Statistic blocks carry a minimum base. A big number is the most-screenshotted thing we produce; one derived from four people travels further than the caveat does.
  • State the disclosure treatment in the provenance chip.
  • Decide disclosure-safe granularity before designing to a granularity, not after.

14Documents, PDFs and HTML

Word documents

  • Real named styles only, and the styles are the roles. Table 8.2 names the Word style each text style becomes: Heading 1 to Heading 4, Subtitle, Normal, Quote, Intense Quote, Caption, Footer, TOC 1, and the new styles Label, Small, Key statement and File reference. Never direct character formatting.
  • Heading 1 to Heading 4 in a logical hierarchy. There is no Heading 5 or 6.
  • Set the document title, author or organisation, and language in properties.
  • Use built-in list styles, indented.
  • One table style, with Header Row and First Column on; the header row repeats across pages. Borders at the four weights only: ¾, 1½, 3 and 6pt.
  • Do not use spaces, tabs or blank paragraphs for layout.
  • Use page breaks rather than repeated returns.
  • Avoid essential information in headers or footers only.
  • Run the Microsoft Accessibility Checker and manually check complex layouts.
  • White ground, not chalk — Word and print handle white more predictably, and partners will edit it.

PowerPoint

  • Every slide carries a unique, descriptive title. It may be positioned off-canvas or hidden. It may not be absent — it is how screen-reader users navigate a deck, and the title list doubles as the deck's outline.
  • Set reading order explicitly in the Selection Pane, on every slide. Reading order follows shape-creation order and bears no relation to visual position. Decorative shapes marked decorative, and last.
  • Build on restyled master layouts, never manually placed text boxes. Built-in layouts keep reading order aligned with visual order.
  • No text box sized to its text. A substituted face widens the same string by roughly a third. Font embedding prevents most substitution; this is the second line of defence.
  • Tables on slides only in decks that are sent and read. A projected deck puts its table in the leave-behind. A deck that is read on screen may carry one, using the Table pattern in section 10.
  • Run the Accessibility Checker before export. Decks leave as tagged PDF; the .pptx goes only to people who must edit it.

PDFs

  • Export from a structured source; do not print to PDF.
  • Verify tags, headings, reading order, links, alt text, title and language.
  • Use bookmarks in longer reports.
  • Ensure text is selectable and searchable.
  • Check zoom, reflow and page order.
  • Provide another accessible format where a fixed-layout PDF is not enough.

Long documents

  • The conclusion sits in the first screen, in every format.
  • Headings state findings, not topics. “Referrals fell 34%” not “Referral trends”. A contents list built from finding-headings is a readable summary, which is what most readers use it as.
  • No skipped heading levels. H2 to H4 breaks outline navigation.
  • Real bookmarks in every PDF, generated from heading styles — not a typeset contents page.

Mandated structures

Before designing, establish whether the structure is mandated, expected or free. Where a funder or commissioner names a model — a Five Case business case, an evaluation framework, their own form or response schedule — follow it exactly. Brand expression lives inside the required structure, never in place of it. A bid can be on-brand, accessible and beautifully set, and still be marked down for answering in the wrong shape.

HTML

  • Make HTML the primary public format where practical.
  • Use semantic headings, lists, tables, landmarks and descriptive links.
  • Preserve keyboard focus, zoom and reflow.
  • Embed fonts as base64 in any self-contained deliverable. Never link a web font service — it fails silently and falls back without warning.

15Known gaps

Still open

When there is no rule. Say so first. Build the nearest thing from the voices, the sizes, the lines, the components and the colours as they are — never a new colour, size, weight or typeface, never a browser default. Show it as an option with what it costs, mark it provisional in the artefact, and log it with the surface it came from. The gap closes when a decision is made against a real case, not when the output ships.

1 · Diagrams. There is no generic diagram kit, and there will not be one: a kit of nodes and arrows produces the default flowchart, which claims an order or a cause whether or not there is one. Name the job first (bound, relate, decompose, sequence, diverge, converge) and build the diagram from the containment treatments in section 09 and the chart ramp in section 12. Never use PowerPoint SmartArt defaults.

2 · Office templates. The Word styles are named in Table 8.2 but the Word template, PowerPoint master and Excel template generated from them do not exist yet. The adapters that build single documents carry style sets of their own until they do.

3 · Dashboards. No dashboard system exists yet, and one should not be built casually. Until it does: a dashboard is only justified where research shows users need to explore, where the data updates automatically, where users genuinely need different cuts, and where there is funding to maintain it beyond launch. All four. Otherwise the answer is a release, a report, or an accessible spreadsheet. If one is built, the default view must answer the main question before any filter is touched, the whole thing must work from the keyboard including the charts, and disclosure thresholds must be enforced at query time on every filter combination — not just the default view.

4 · Public severity marks. Internal status chips carry a word on a fill. A public document has no coloured severity mark until one is decided against a real case. Never RAG tags.

5 · Other button styles and the icon set. One button, one text action and one search icon exist.

6 · Ink and charcoal. The two text colours cannot be told apart on a chalk ground. Both stay until decided.

7 · Chart marks. The big figure in a statistic and the labels and values inside a chart are sized to their chart, outside the six sizes. They move onto the styles when the chart set is next revised.

16The eight tests

TestQuestion
Committee-room testIs it credible, decision-ready and defensible?
Dancefloor testDoes it retain cultural truth and avoid institutionalising the culture?
Phone testCan someone understand it quickly on a small screen?
Screen-reader testDoes the meaning survive without the visual treatment?
Hostile-reader testAre the claims, sources and assumptions defensible under scrutiny?
Partner testDoes the language make room for collaboration and recognise others' contribution?
Paid-work testCan the reader understand what Nightlife Culture can do and what to ask for?
Carly testDoes this contain an actual idea, argument or observation that sounds like it comes from somebody who knows the culture and understands the system?

The Carly test

Does this contain an actual idea, argument or observation that sounds like it comes from somebody who knows the culture and understands the system? Ask:

  • Could any competent cultural consultancy have written this?
  • Have we kept the argument, or replaced it with a general statement?
  • Is there something specific, unexpected, insightful or challenging here?
  • Have we lost the humour, energy or conviction of the original?
  • Does the language respect the intelligence of both the cultural community and the institutional audience?
  • Have we made the writing safer at the expense of making it meaningful?

If any consultancy could have written it, go back to the source. Not to add more personality: to recover the thinking that got removed.

17Do and do not

DoDo not
Lead with value, people and possibility.Use abundance framing to hide structural problems.
Use precise policy and academic terms when the context requires them.Dumb down complex ideas or inflate simple ones.
Translate technical language for broader audiences.Assume specialist language communicates itself.
Use evidence in service of culture and decisions.Let research language replace sector knowledge.
Treat accessibility as part of the brand system.Treat accessibility as a final compliance check.
Use brand strongly in rhythm, layout, typography and decoration.Make essential meaning depend on colour, image or layout.
Name sources, limitations and assumptions.Let polished design overstate confidence.
Make the next step clear.End with vague “support” or “engagement” language.
Contain with colour and space.Outline every panel in black.
Use the chart ramp for data.Encode data in the brand accents.
Embed fonts in every deliverable.Link a web font service and assume it loaded.
Leave half the canvas empty.Reduce type to fit more copy on a slide.

Line height resolved to a single 1.5–1.6 floor, stated once. Document body minimum raised to 12pt. Caps mechanism specified as formatting, never typed. Separator required on segmented charts. Disclosure control added. PowerPoint, long-form and mandated-structure sections added. Room rule added for slide grounds. Dashboard gate added to Known gaps.
1.2August 2026Line height scoped by style class and context. 1.5–1.6 was resolved in v1.1 as a single value; that is the running-prose value and was never a rule for table cells, captions, display or statistics. A scoped table now sets each. Table cells 1.25–1.35 — tight is more readable, because rows are read across. Only running prose is Fixed.
1.3August 2026Logo section replaced in full. The wordmark is an outlined asset and is never re-set as live type — the previous section described it as “Archivo Black, tight leading” and rendered four live-type specimens, which is the failure the rule exists to prevent. Adds the four SVG variants, the measurements from the printed card (NIGHTLIFE 32.09pt, CULTURE 33.41pt, set at different sizes so both lines justify to the same width), ten rules, minimum size, clear space, and the instruction to stop rather than improvise a variant. Ground swatches now show which file to place, and deliberately draw no wordmark.
1.4August 2026The wordmark is now placed, not typeset. Masthead and footer carry the outlined SVG inline. The four variants were regenerated from the section 11 measurements and verified against them — NIGHTLIFE 171.92pt, CULTURE 171.19pt, justifying to 0.42%. Tracking differs per line (−0.0872em / −0.0264em), which is what lets two sizes finish at one width.
1.4.1August 2026The colour rule corrected. The one-line law — “every accent is a black-text surface; every ground is a white-text surface” — was false for two of the four grounds (white on chalk 1.11:1, white on white 1.00:1) and contradicted this guide’s own token cards in the same section. Section 07 now states the per-ground rule: accents take ink text; each ground declares its own — white on blue and ink, ink on chalk and white. Recorded as contradiction X-02 in the v1.4 register; the design-system validator fails a build on white text over a light ground.
1.4.2September 2026Slides learned from live work. Section 10 replaced: the generated slide grid and its examples gave way to twelve patterns taken from a real deck (Artists Make Great Places v2.0), at that deck's sizes — body 18pt, titles 36–43pt. Charcoal is a text colour, never a ground; ink is the dark ground. Caps floor 16pt. Any accent may carry the wordmark: a logotype is exempt from text contrast, a logged break (NC-BRK-03). The dense layout tier is closed; the diagram gap restated as the design system now handles it. Tables: the component library's table is the house style for documents, including this guide; the slide table is for presentations, allowed in decks that are sent and read.
1.55 October 2026One rule for all type, four weights of line. Section 08 replaced: every text style is one of five voices at one of six sizes, twenty-six named styles with the Word style each becomes, generated from the design system's tokens; H4 added with a blue bar above it and named as the floor; the label decided at 12px (10pt); italic for a short run inside a paragraph, no monospace. Section 09: the containment lines become four weights — hairline 1px, table line 2px, rule 4px, callout 8px — and the takeaway, quotation, key statement, subtitle, evidence mark, recommendation, working note, status chips, button, search field, collapsible heading and contents are specified. Section 04: night time is two words. Section 14: the Word styles are the type styles. Section 15 rewritten with the rule for when there is no rule. This guide is set on the design system's own stylesheet for the first time, so it is built the way the system builds everything; its pull quotes are now the takeaway style. Decided with Carly Heath across seven rendered review rounds, 4–5 October 2026; the reasoning is in the design system's docs/changelog.md.
1.5.114 October 2026The voice, rewritten from Rowan's review. Section 03 opens with a new passage. The six voice qualities become eight characteristics, with three voice modes; the emotional arc is a guiding philosophy, not a running order. Section 04 protects questions, deliberate repetition, humour and metaphor, adds before-and-after examples of flattening, and distinguishes cultural value from cultural contribution. Section 00 protects original thinking and states that voice is not stylistic preference. Sections 01 and 02 add what we're here to change and how we build an argument. Section 06 separates the accuracy of evidence from the strength of the argument. Section 16 adds the Carly test.
